But one who is delivering a narrative about him has no business being precise about any of these things, as indeed Herodotus and Thucydides did, each of whom set out to tell of the Cylonian pollution.

In matters of diction one must observe not to use synonyms; for words having the same force make the speech longer with no need, as in Demosthenes in the second Olynthiac: it seems altogether like some divine and heaven-sent benefaction. Nor should one make a phrase in place of a single word — for instance, instead of 'he died,' 'he departed from life,' and all such expressions. Further, whoever wishes to report concisely must strip away along with the rest everything that is understood; and he should use simple words rather than compound ones, and shorter rather than longer, when they signify the same thing. Yet one must take care not to fall unawares, through the desire for conciseness, into vulgarity or obscurity.
verses.greek: Ὁμοίως δὲ ἔσται καὶ σύντομος ἡ διήγησις ἐκ τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τῆς λέξεως. ἔστι γὰρ ἡ συντομία λόγος τὰ καιριώτατα τῶν πραγμάτων σημαίνων, μήτε προστιθεὶς τὸ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον μήτε ἀφαιρῶν τὸ ἀναγκαῖον κατὰ τὰ πράγματα καὶ τὴν λέξιν. ἐκ μὲν οὖν τῶν πραγμάτων, ὅταν μήτε συλλαμβάνωμεν ἅμα τὰ πολλὰ πράγματα, μήθʼ ἑτέροις ἐπεμβάλλωμεν, παραλείπωμέν τε ὅσα συνυπακούεσθαι δοκεῖ, μήτε πόρρωθεν ἀρχώμεθα, μήτε εἰς τὰ παρέλκοντα τὸν λόγον καταναλίσκωμεν, ὡς οἱ μετὰ τὰ πράγματα εἰωθότες διηγεῖσθαι. ταῦτα γὰρ ἂν ἴσως ἱστορίᾳ πρέποι, τό τε μηκύνειν καὶ τὸ πόρρωθεν ἄρχεσθαι καὶ ἐπεξεργάζεσθαί τινα τῶν παρέργων εἶναι δοκούντων. διήγησιν δὲ λέγων τις πρὸς τὸ κεφάλαιον τοῦ ὅλου πράγματος, ὃ προὔθετο, ἀποβλέπειν ὀφείλει τὰ εἰς τοῦτο συντελοῦντα μόνα ἐν τῇ διηγήσει παραλαμβάνων, οἷον τὶ τοῦ Κύλωνος, εἰ μέν τις ἱστορίαν περὶ αὐτοῦ συγγράφει, προσήκει καὶ τίνων προγόνων ἦν καὶ τίνος πατρός τε καὶ μητρὸς καὶ ἄλλα πάμπολλα λέγειν, τό τε ἀγώνισμα, ὃ ἠγωνίζετο ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ, καὶ ὅσας νίκας ἀνείλετο, καὶ τὰς Ὀλυμπιάδας ὀνομάζειν ἐφʼ ὧν ἐνίκα διήγημα δέ τις περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγων οὐδὲν τῶν τοιούτων ἀκριβολογεῖσθαι δίκαιός ἐστι, καθάπερ ἐποίησεν Ἡρόδοτός τε καὶ Θουκυδίδης, ἑκάτερος τὸ Κυλώνειον ἄγος εἰπεῖν προθέμενος. ἐν δὲ τοῖς κατὰ τὴν λέξιν παρατηρητέον καὶ τὸ μήτε συνωνύμοις χρῆσθαι· τὰ γὰρ τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχοντα δύναμιν ὀνόματα μακρότερον ποιεῖ τὸν λόγον οὐδὲν δέον. ὡς παρὰ Δημοσθένει ἐν τῶν Ὀλυνθιακῶν δευτέρῳ· δαιμονίᾳ τινὶ καὶ θείᾳ παντάπασιν ἔοικεν εὐεργεσίᾳ· μήτε λόγον ἀντὶ ὀνόματος ποιεῖν, οἶον ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀπέθανεν ἐξέλιπε τὸν βίον, καὶ ὅσα τούτοις ὅμοια. ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ συνυπακουόμενα πάντως συμπεριαιρετέον τῷ συντόμως ἀπαγγέλλειν βουλομένῳ, χρηστέον δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἁπλοῖς ὀνόμασι μᾶλλον ἢ τοῖς συνθέτοις, καὶ τοῖς βραχυτέροις μᾶλλον ἢ τοῖς μακροτέροις, ὅταν τὸ αὐτὸ σημαίνωσιν εὐλαβητέον δὲ ὅμως μὴ λάθῃ τις ἐπιθυμίᾳ συντομίας εἰς ἰδιωτισμὸν ἢ ἀσάφειαν ἐκπεσών.
verses.heading: Conciseness

verses.text:
For the narrative to be plausible, one must adopt expressions proper to the persons and the matters and the places and the occasions, and matters that are likely and consistent with one another. One must also add the causes briefly to the narrative, and state what is disbelieved in a credible way; and in general one should aim at what is fitting to the person and to the other elements of the narrative, both in the matters and in the diction.

Our example will be the narrative at the beginning of the second book of Thucydides about the Plataeans and the Thebans. For it was likely that the Thebans, being always at variance with the Plataeans, on learning that there would be a war, should wish to seize Plataea in advance while it was still peace; and that, having so resolved, they should not make the attempt openly but on a moonless night; and besides this, that they should have some of the Plataeans who would open the gates for them, no guard having been posted because of the treaty; and that those who betrayed the city did so for the sake of a private enmity toward certain of the citizens, whom they meant to destroy when this happened — not that the Thebans had betrayed them.

It is plausible, too, that the Plataeans, perceiving that the city had been suddenly seized by the enemy, supposed because of the night that far more had entered, and so came to terms; but afterwards, realizing that they were not many, attacked them. And the uproar is altogether most plausible: the Plataeans falling upon the Thebans, and at the same time the women and the household slaves from the houses raising a shout and a wailing and pelting the Thebans with stones and tiles; and a heavy rain having come on in the night, many of the Thebans being pursued through mud and darkness and unable to escape through inexperience of the roads.

It is plausible also that someone shut the gates, using the butt-spike of a javelin instead of the pin for the bar; and much more plausible still is the matter of the woman who gave the axe. For it was likely that a woman living near deserted gates, seeing the enemy shut in, should be afraid that, despairing of safety and reduced to desperation, they might turn to doing harm — most of all to whomever they could, but first of all to the neighbouring houses. I say nothing of the fact that it was like a woman to pity even enemies who had been beaten. And so with all the rest, that we may not speak at length.
verses.greek: Ὑπὲρ γε μὴν τοῦ πιθανὴν εἶναι τὴν διήγησιν παραληπτέον λέξεις μὲν προσφυεῖς τοῖς τε προσώποις καὶ τοῖς πράγμασι καὶ τοῖς τόποις καὶ τοῖς καιροῖς· πράγματα δὲ ὅσα εἰκότα ἐστὶ καὶ ἀλλήλοις ἀκόλουθα. δεῖ δὲ καὶ τὰς αἰτίας βραχέως προστιθέναι τῇ διηγήσει, καὶ τὸ ἀπιστούμενον πιστῶς λέγειν, καὶ ἀπλῶς στοχάζεσθαι προσήκει τοῦ πρέποντος τῷ τε προσώπῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις στοιχείοις τῆς διηγήσεως κατά τε τὰ πράγματα καὶ κατὰ τὴν λέξιν. παράδειγμα δὲ ἡμῖν ἔσται τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆ, δευτέρας τοῦ Θουκυδίδου περὶ Πλαταιέων καὶ Θηβαίων διήγημα· εἰκὸς γὰρ ἦν τούς Θηβαίους ἀεὶ διαφόρους ὄντας τοῖς Πλαταιεῦσι μαθόντας, ὅτι ἔσοιτο πόλεμος. ἐθελῆσαι προκαταλαβεῖν τὴν Πλάταιαν ἔτι ἐν εἰρήνῃ ταῦτα δὲ βουλευσαμένους ἐκ μὲν τοῦ φανεροῦ μὴ ἐπιχειρεῖν, νυκτὶ δὲ ἀσελήνῳ ἐπιχειρῆσαι, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἔχειν τινὰς Πλαταιέων, οἳ καὶ ἀνοίξουσιν αὐτοῖς τὰς πύλας μηδεμιᾶς φυλακῆς προκαθεστηκυίας διὰ τὰς σπονδάς, τούς τε προδιδόντας ἰδίου ἕνεκα ἐχθροῦ πρός τινας τῶν πολιτῶν, οὓς ᾤοντο διαφθεῖραι τούτων γινομένων, ἀλλὰ μὴ τὸ τοὺς Θηβαίους προδεδωκέναι. πιθανὸν δὲ τὸ μὲν αἰσθανομένους τούς Πλαταιέας προκατειλημμένην τὴν πόλιν ἐξαπιναίως ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων, νομίσαι τε διὰ τὴν νύκτα πολλῷ πλείους εἰσεληλυθέναι, πρὸς ξύμβασίν τε χωρῆσαι, ὕστερον δὲ κατανοήσαντας οὐ πολλούς ὄντας ἐπιθέσθαι αὐτοῖς. καὶ θόρυβος δὲ πάνυ πιθανώτατος τῶν μὲν Πλαταιέων προσβαλλόντων τοῖς Θηβαίοις καὶ τῶν γυναικῶν καὶ τῶν οἰκετῶν ἅμα ἀπὸ τῶν οἰκιῶν κραυγῇ τε καὶ ὀλολυγῇ χρωμένων λίθοις τε καὶ κεράμοις βαλλόντων τούς Θηβαίους, καὶ ὑετοῦ πολλοῦ ἐπιγενομένου νυκτός, πολλούς τῶν Θηβαίων διά τε πηλοῦ καὶ σκότους διωκομένων, ἀπειρίᾳ δὲ τῶν ὁδῶν οὐ δυναμένων ἐκφυγεῖν. πιθανὸν δὲ τὸ καὶ κλεῖσαί τινα τὰς πύλας στυρακίῳ ἀκοντίου ἀντὶ βαλάνου χρησάμενον εἰς τὸν μοχλόν, πολὺ δὲ πιθανώτερον τὸ τῆς δούσης γυναικὸς πέλεκυν εἰκὸς γὰρ ἦν γυναῖκα πρὸς ἐρήμοις πύλαις οἰκοῦσαν, θεασαμένην τοὺς πολεμίους ἀποκεκλεισμένους φοβηθῆναι, μὴ ἀπελπίσαντας τὴν σωτηρίαν καὶ εἰς ἀπόνοιαν περιστάντας τραπέσθαι ἐπὶ τὸ κακῶς ποιεῖν, μάλιστα μὲν οὖν οὓς ἂν δύνωνται, πολὺ δὲ πρότερον τὰς πλησίον οἰκίας· ἐῶ γὰρ ὅτι κατὰ γυναῖκα ἦν ἐλεῆσαι καὶ πολεμίους νενικημένους· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα, ἵνα μὴ μακρολογῶμεν.
verses.heading: Plausibility, with Thucydides at Plataea as the model

verses.text:
The exercise on the narrative is not of a single form. Just as with the fable, it is recited and inflected and interwoven with a fable, and it is compressed and expanded; further, in the recitation we alter the order of the headings; and besides this it is possible, while keeping the same order, to make the phrasing in many and varied ways. Further still, one may add a comment while narrating, and interweave two or even three narratives with one another in the recitation; and after all these, one may refute and confirm.

Now concerning recitation and inflection and interweaving, and further compression and expansion, we have spoken in the section on fables. The inversion of the order we shall accomplish in many ways. For it is possible to begin from the middle and run back to the beginning, and then to come down to the last events — which is what Homer did in the Odyssey. For he began from the time when Odysseus was with Calypso, then ran back to the beginning with a polished management of his material, since he made Odysseus narrate his own affairs to the Phaeacians; and then, joining on the remaining narrative, he ended with the last events, up to Odysseus' killing of the suitors and his making of friendship with their parents. Thucydides too, beginning from the affairs at Epidamnus, ran back to the fifty years, and then came down to the Peloponnesian War.

It is possible also to begin from the last events and come to the middle, and so to arrive at the beginning — which Herodotus teaches us in his third book, speaking thus: Cambyses, sending a herald to Egypt, asked Amasis for his daughter; and he asked on the advice of an Egyptian man, who did this out of a grudge against Amasis, because Amasis had torn him from his wife and children and handed him over to the Persians. Then he narrates the causes as well: that the king of the Persians had asked from the king of the Egyptians for an eye-doctor, whoever was best. For the natural order of the narrative would have been first to tell of the eye-disease of the king of the Persians, and how, sending to Egypt, he asked from the ruler there for an eye-doctor, and that man sent him up; then that the doctor, taking it hard to be parted from wife and children, avenged himself on the man who had given him up, by advising the king of the Persians to ask for a daughter from the king of the Egyptians, so that either by giving her he should be grieved, or by not giving her should incur enmity.

It is possible, further, to begin from the middle and come to the end, and there to stop; and again to begin from the last events and run back to the beginning and stop at the middle; and further to begin from the first events and pass over to the last, and to cease at the middle.
verses.greek: Οὐ μονοειδὴς δὲ τοῦ διηγήματος ἡ γυμνασία, ἀλλὰ καθάπερ ὁ μῦθος, καὶ ἀπαγγέλλεται καὶ κλίνεται καὶ συμπλέκεται μύθῳ, συστέλλεταί τε καὶ ἐπεκτείνεται, ἔτι δὲ κατὰ τὴν ἀπαγγελίαν ἐναλλάττομεν τῶν κεφαλαίων τὴν τάξιν, καὶ πρός τούτοις ἐστὶ καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν τάξιν φυλάττουσι κατὰ πολλοὺς καὶ ποικίλους τρόπους ποιεῖσθαι τὴν φράσιν· ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἐπιφωνεῖν διηγούμενον καὶ συμπλέκειν ἀλλήλαις δύο ἢ καὶ τρεῖς διηγήσεις κατὰ τὴν ἀπαγγελίαν ἐφʼ ἅπασι δὲ τό τε ἀνασκευάζειν καὶ κατασκευάζειν. περὶ μὲν οὖν ἀπαγγελίας καὶ κλίσεως καὶ συμπλοκῆς, ἔτι δὲ συστολῆς τε καὶ ἐπεκτάσεως ἐν τῷ περὶ μύθων εἴρηται, τὴν δὲ ἀναστροφὴν τῆς τάξεως πολλαχῶς ποιησόμεθα· καὶ γὰρ ἀπὸ τῶν μέσων ἐστὶν ἀρξάμενον ἐπὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀναδραμεῖν, εἶτα ἐπὶ τὰ τελευταῖα καταντῆσαι, ὅπερ ἐν Ὀδυσσείᾳ Ὅμηρος πεποίηκεν· ἤρξατο μὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῶν χρόνων, καθʼ οὓς Ὀδυσσεὺς ἦν παρὰ Καλυψοῖ, εἶτα ἀνέδραμεν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν μετά τινος οἰκονομίας γλαφυρᾶς· ἐποίει γὰρ τὸν Ὀδυσσέα τοῖς Φαίαξι τὰ καθʼ ἑαυτὸν διηγούμενον, εἶτα συνάψας τὴν λοιπὴν διήγησιν ἔληξεν εἰς τὰ τελευταῖα, μέχρι τοὺς μνηστῆρας ἀπέκτεινεν Ὀδυσσεύς, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς γονέας αὐτῶν φιλίαν ἐποιήσατο. καὶ Θουκυδίδης δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν περὶ Ἐπίδαμνον ἀρξάμενος ἀνέδραμεν ἐπὶ τὴν πεντηκονταετίαν, ἔπειτα κατῆλθεν ἐπὶ τὸν Πελοποννησιακὸν πόλεμον. ἔξεστι δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν τελευταίων ἀρξάμενον ἐλθεῖν ἐπὶ τὰ μέσα, καὶ οὕτως ἐπὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν καταντῆσαι, ὅπερ Ἡρόδοτος διὰ τῆς τρίτης ἡμᾶς διδάσκει λέγων οὕτω· πέμψας Καμβύσης εἰς Αἴγυπτον κήρυκα αἴτεε Ἄμασιν θυγατέρα, αἴτεε δὲ ἐκ συμβουλῆς ἀνδρὸς Αἰγυπτίου, ὃς μεμφόμενος Ἄμασιν ἔπρηξε ταῦτα, ὅτι μιν ἀποσπάσας γυναικός τε καὶ τέκνων ἔκδοτον ἐποίησεν εἰς Πέρσας· εἶτα καὶ τὰ αἴτια διηγεῖται, ὅτι ὁ τῶν Περσῶν βασιλεύς τήκει παρὰ τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως ἰατρὸν ὀφθαλμῶν, ὃς εἴη ἄριστος· ἡ γὰρ κατὰ φύσιν ἦν τάξις τῆς διηγήσεως πρῶτον μὲν τὴν ὀφθαλμίαν εἰπεῖν τοῦ Περσῶν βασιλέως, καὶ ὡς πέμψας εἰς Αἴγυπτον ᾔτησε παρὰ τοῦ βασιλεύοντος ἐκεῖ ἰατρὸν ὀφθαλμῶν, ὁ δὲ τοῦτον ἀναπέμπει, ἔπειτα ὅτι χαλεπῶς φέρων ὁ ἰατρὸς γυναικός τε καὶ παίδων ἀπολειφθεὶς ἠμύνατο τὸν ἐκδόντα, συμβουλεύσας τῷ Περσῶν βασιλεῖ αἰτῆσαι θυγατέρα παρὰ τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως, ἵνα ἢ δοὺς ἀνιῷτο, ἢ μὴ δοὺς ἀπέχθοιτο. ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν μέσων ἀρξάμενον ἐπὶ τὴν τελευτὴν ἐλθεῖν, εἶτα ἐν τούτοις λῆξαι. καὶ πάλιν ἀπὸ τῶν τελευταίων ἀρξάμενον ἀναδραμεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν καὶ λῆξαι εἰς τὰ μέσα, καὶ ἔτι ἀπὸ τῶν πρώτων ἀρξάμενον μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ τὰ τελευταῖα, καὶ ἐν τοῖς μέσοις παύσασθαι.
verses.heading: The forms of the exercise; inverting the order

verses.text:
So much, then, for the inversion of the order. Since we are accustomed to bring matters out sometimes as making a statement, sometimes as doing something more than stating; sometimes as asking a question, at other times as inquiring, and sometimes as raising a difficulty; at one time as giving a command, at another as praying; now as swearing an oath, now as addressing someone; at another time as supposing, and sometimes as conversing — it is possible to bring out narratives in all these manners, varying them.

Thucydides, then, at the beginning of the second book of his Histories, brought out this narrative in the manner of one making a statement: Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians.

But if we should wish to do something more than state, we shall say thus: The coming of the Thebans to Plataea proved, it seems, the cause of great events for the Athenians and the Spartans and the allies on either side; for Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia. And so we shall join on the rest of the narrative.

If we should wish to ask a question, we shall say thus: Is it then true that Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia? And in this interrogative fashion we shall go through what follows. We should inquire thus: Who were the Theban men, a little more than three hundred, who entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia? And we shall bring in the rest by way of inquiry.

Raising a difficulty and asking a question differ in no way in the utterance, and therefore we shall be content with one of them; for whether we ask or raise a difficulty, we shall bring it out thus: Is sleeplessness the most talkative of all things? They seem to differ in that the one who asks seeks an answer, while the one who raises a difficulty does not altogether do so, but is merely at a loss within himself.

If we should wish to give a command, we shall do it thus. We shall suppose, in the last part of the narrative, after the destruction of those who entered Plataea, someone exhorting either the Thebans or the Plataeans, in this way: Come, men of Plataea, show yourselves worthy of your city, and of your ancestors who fought against the Persians and Mardonius, and of those who lie buried in your land. Show the Thebans that they act unjustly in thinking you should obey them and be their slaves, and in forcing you by war against your will, contrary to the oaths and the treaties — a little more than three hundred of them, who entered under arms about the time of first sleep into your city, which is an ally of the Athenians. And in the same way we shall narrate what follows as addressed to the Plataeans.

If we should suppose the exhortation to be made to the Thebans, we shall say thus: Come, men of Thebes, show yourselves worthy of yourselves and of your fathers and of the rule you hold over all Boeotia; and show the Plataeans that, being your slaves, they have not only run away to the Athenians but have also destroyed men of yours, a little more than three hundred, who came under arms about the time of first sleep into their Plataea. And in this manner we shall narrate the rest.

It is possible also to make a command in this way, if we should suppose someone commanding the Thebans, before the entry into Plataea took place, to do the very things they did: Come, men of Thebes, let men of yours, a little more than three hundred, enter under arms about the time of first sleep into your own Plataea, which is now an ally of the Athenians. And we shall go through what follows in this manner, so far as it admits of it.

If we should pray, we shall say thus: Would that Theban men, a little more than three hundred, had never entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians. And to the end we shall narrate in the manner of one praying.

It is not obscure in what manner the narrative will be brought out in the form of an oath. The form of address we pass over, because we have already handed it on earlier, among the inflections by cases, under the vocative.

Supposing, we shall say thus: Let us suppose that Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians; and that Naucleides and those with him opened the gates for them, no guard having been posted because of the treaty — and so with what follows.

If we should wish to report in dialogue, we shall suppose certain persons conversing with one another about what was done, the one teaching and the other learning what had happened. For example: Often before now it has occurred to you to ask me about what befell the Thebans and the Plataeans at Plataea; and now too I would gladly hear of it, if you have time to narrate it. — But indeed there is time, and I am telling you at once, if, as you say, you have a desire to hear about these things. The Thebans, being always at variance with the Plataeans, wished to seize Plataea in advance while it was peace. So men of theirs, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into the city, which was an ally of the Athenians. — How then, when it was night and the gates were shut, and moreover a guard was posted, did they easily enter unnoticed? — You have anticipated me a little, since I too was about to say that men opened the gates for them, Naucleides and those with him, no guard having been posted because of the peace — and so on. In the same manner we shall go through it, asking and answering according to the rule of dialectic.

Further, in stating matters we sometimes affirm — for instance, Theon is conversing. But it is possible to bring out narratives not only affirming but also denying: affirming, as we said Thucydides brought out the narrative; denying, for instance — Neither did Theban men, a little more than three hundred, enter under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians, nor did Naucleides and those with him open the gates; and so to the end.

There is also another manner, called asyndeton, when we leave out the connectives that bind the phrasing together — for instance: Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, an ally of the Athenians; Naucleides and those with him opened the gates for them; they placed their arms in the market-place. And similarly with what follows. So too in Demosthenes: Amphipolis, Pydna, Potidaea, Halonnesus — I mention none of these. And again: But he is gone to the Hellespont; earlier he came against Ambracia; he holds Elis, so great a city in the Peloponnese; he plotted against Megara the other day.

It is possible also to interweave these manners with one another and to make a mixture of two or more, so as to report some parts of the narrative in the manner of one making a statement, others without connectives, and others in whatever way one wishes, varying the phrasing.
verses.greek: Κατὰ μὲν οὖν τὴν ἀναστροφὴν τῆς τάξεως οὕτως· ἐπεὶ δὲ εἰώθαμεν ἐκφέρειν τὰ πράγματα ἐνίοτε μὲν ὡς ἀποφαινόμενοι, ἐνίοτε δὲ ὡς πλέον τι τοῦ ἀποφαίνεσθαι ποιοῦντες, καὶ ἐνίοτε μὲν ὡς ἐρωτῶντες, ἄλλοτε δὲ ὡς πυνθανόμενοι, ἔσθʼ ὅτε δὲ ὡς ἐπαποροῦντες, καί ἄλλοτε μὲν ὡς προστάττοντες, ἄλλοτε δὲ ὡς εὐχόμενοι, καί ποτε μὲν ὡς ὀμνύοντες, ποτὲ δὲ ὡς προσαγορεύοντες, ἄλλοτε δὲ ὑποτιθέμενοι, ποτὲ δὲ προσδιαλεγόμενοι ἐνδέχεται γὰρ κατὰ πάντας τούτους τοὺς τρόπους ἐκφέρειν ποικίλλοντας τὰς διηγήσεις· Θουκυδίδης μὲν οὖν ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς δευτέρας τῶν ἱστοριῶν κατὰ τὸν τοῦ ἀποφαινομένου τρόπον ἐξήνεγκεν τὴν διήγησιν ταύτην· Θηβαίων ἄνδρες ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας, οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων συμμαχίδα. ἡμεῖς δὲ εἰ βουλοίμεθα πλέον τι τοῦ ἀποφαίνεσθαι ποιεῖν, οὕτως ἐροῦμεν· μεγάλων ὡς ἔοικε πραγμάτων αἰτία γέγονεν Ἀθηναίοις καὶ Λακεδαιμονίοις καὶ τοῖς ἐξ ἑκάστων συμμάχοις Θηβαίων εἰς Πλάταιαν ἄφιξις Θηβαίων γὰρ ἄνδρες ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας καὶ οὕτω τὰ λοιπὰ τῆς διηγήσεως συνάψομεν. εἰ δὲ ἐρωτᾶν βουλοίμεθα, οὕτως ἐροῦμεν· ἀρά γε ἀληθές ἐστιν ὅτι Θηβαίων ἄνδρες ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας; καὶ οὕτως ἐρωτηματικῶς τὰ μετὰ ταῦτα διελευσόμεθα. οὕτω δʼ ἂν πυθοίμεθα, τίνες ἦσαν οἱ Θηβαίων ἄνδρες, οἵ ὀλίγῳ πλείους ἦσαν τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σύν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας; καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ πυνθανόμενοι ἐποίσομεν. τὸ δὲ ἐπαπορεῖν καὶ τὸ ἐρωτᾶν κατὰ μὲν τὴν προφορὰν οὐδὲν ἀλλήλων διήνεγκε, διόπερ τῷ ἑτέρῳ αὐτῶν ἀρκεσθησόμεθα ἐάν τε γὰρ ἐρωτῶμεν, ἐάν τε ἐπαπορῶμεν, οὕτως ἐξοίσομεν· ἆρʼ ἔστι πάντων ἀγρυπνία λαλίστατον; διαφέρειν δὲ δοκεῖ, ὅτι ὁ μὲν ἐρωτῶν ἀπόκρισιν ἐπιζητεῖ ὁ δὲ ἐπαπορῶν οὐ πάντως, ἀλλὰ μόνον πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀπορεῖ. εἰ δὲ προστάττειν βουλοίμεθα, οὕτω ποιήσομεν ὑποθησόμεθα γὰρ ἐν τοῖς τελευταίοις τῆς διηγήσεως. μετὰ τὴν τῶν εἰσελθόντων εἰς Πλαταιὰς ἀναίρεσιν, ἕνα τινὰ παραινοῦντα ἢ τοῖς Θηβαίοις ἢ τοῖς Πλαταιεῦσι οὕτως· ἄγετε, ὧ Πλαταιεῖς, ὅπως ἄξιοι τῆς πόλεως ἔσεσθε, καὶ τῶν προγόνων πρὸς Πέρσας τε καὶ Μαρδόνιον ἠγωνισμένων, καὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ κειμένων. δείξατε τοῖς Θηβαίοις, ὅτι μὴ δίκαια ποιοῦσιν ἀξιοῦντες μὲν ὑμᾶς σφίσιν ὑπακούειν καὶ δουλεύειν, οὐκ ἐθέλοντας δὲ πολέμῳ βιαζόμενοι παρὰ τοὺς ὅρκους καὶ τὰς συνθήκας, ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων, εἶτα εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς τὴν πόλιν τὴν ὑμετέραν οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων συμμαχίδα· καὶ ὡσαύτως τὰ ἑξῆς ὡς πρὸς Πλαταιεῖς διηγησόμεθα. εἰ δὲ ὑποθοίμεθα τὴν παρακέλευσιν γίνεσθαι πρὸς τοὺς Θηβαίους, οὕτως ἐροῦμεν ἄγετε, ὦ Θηβαῖοι, ὅπως φανήσεσθε αὐτῶν τε καὶ τῶν πατέρων ἄξιοι καὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς, ἣν ἔχετε, συμπάσης τῆς Βοιωτίας, καὶ δείξατε τοῖς Πλαταιεῦσιν, ὅτι δοῦλοι ὄντες ὑμέτεροι οὐ μόνον ἀποδεδράκασι πρὸς Ἀθηναίους, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄνδρας ὑμετέρους ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων, ἐλθόντας περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σύν ὅπλοις εἰς τὴν Πλάταιαν τὴν ἑαυτῶν, διέφθειραν. καὶ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ διηγησόμεθα. ἔστι δὲ καὶ οὕτω πρόσταξιν ποιήσασθαι, εἰ ὑποθοίμεθά τινα τοῖς Θηβαίοις, πρὶν γενέσθαι τὴν εἰς Πλάταιαν εἴσοδον, προστάττοντα, ἃ δὴ καὶ ἔπραξαν ἄγετε, ὦ Θηβαῖοι, ὅπως ἄνδρες ἐξ ὑμῶν ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσέλθωσι περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σύν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τὴν ὑμετέραν, νῦν δʼ οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων συμμαχίδα· καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, ὡς ἄν ἐνδέχηται, κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον διεξελευσόμεθα. εἰ δὲ εὐχοίμεθα, οὕτως ἐροῦμεν· εἴθε μηδέποτε Θηβαίων ἄνδρες ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας, οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων συμμαχίδα· καὶ μέχρι τέλους κατὰ τὸν τοῦ εὐχομένου τρόπον διηγησόμεθα. οὐκ ἄδηλος δὲ ὁ τρόπος, πῶς κατὰ τὴν ὀμοτικὴν προφορὰν ἡ διήγησις ἐξενεχθήσεται τὴν δὲ προσαγορευτικὴν παραιτούμεθα, ὅτι καὶ πρότερον ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ τὰς πτώσεις ἐγκλίσεων ἤδη παραδεδώκαμεν ἐπὶ τῆς κλητικῆς. ὑποτιθέμενοι δὲ οὕτως ἐροῦμεν ὑποθώμεθα γάρ, Θηβαίων ἄνδρας, ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων, εἰσελθεῖν περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας, οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων συμμαχίδα ἀνοῖξαι δʼ αὐτοῖς τὰς πύλας Ναυκλείδην τε καὶ τοὺς μετʼ αὐτοῦ μηδεμιᾶς φυλακῆς προκαθεστηκυίας διὰ τὰς σπονδάς, καὶ οὕτω τὰ μετὰ ταῦτα. εἰ δὲ διαλογικῶς ἀπαγγέλλειν βουλοίμεθα, ὑποθησόμεθά τέ τινας ἀλλήλοις διαλεγομένους περὶ τῶν πεπραγμένων, καὶ τὸν μὲν διδάσκοντα τὸν δὲ μανθάνοντα τὰ γεγενημένα, οἷον πολλάκις μέν σε καὶ πρότερον ἐπῆλθεν ἔρεσθαί μοι περὶ τῶν ἐν Πλαταιαῖς συμβεβηκότων Θηβαίοις τε καὶ Πλαταιεῦσιν. ἀτὰρ καὶ νῦν ἡδέως ἄν ἀκούσαιμι, εἴ σοι ἐν καιρῷ ἐστι διηγήσασθαι. ἀλλὰ νὴ Δία καιρός ἐστι, καὶ δὴ καὶ ἤδη σοι λέγω, εἴπερ, ὥς φῃς, ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχεις ἀκοῦσαι περὶ τούτων· Θηβαῖοι γὰρ ἀεὶ διάφοροι ὄντες τοῖς Πλαταιεῦσιν ἐβούλοντο τὴν Πλάταιαν ἐν εἰρήνῃ προκαταλαβεῖν. ἄνδρες οὖν ἐξ αὐτῶν ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς τὴν πόλιν, οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων συμμαχίδα. πῶς οὖν νυκτὸς οὔσης καὶ τῶν πυλῶν κεκλεισμένων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ φυλακῆς καθεστηκυίας ῥᾳδίως ἔλαθον εἰσελθόντες; μικρὸν μὲν ἔφθης, ἐπεὶ καὶ αὐτὸς ἔμελλον εἰπεῖν, ὅτι τὰς πύλας ἀνέῳξαν αὐτοῖς ἄνδρες, Ναυκλείδης τε καὶ οἱ μετʼ αὐτοῦ, φυλακῆς οὐδεμιᾶς προκαθεστηκυίας διὰ τὴν εἰρήνην, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον διεξελευσόμεθα ἐρωτῶντές τε καὶ ἀποκρινόμενοι κατὰ τὸν διαλεκτικὸν νόμον, ἔτι δὲ ἀποφαινόμενοι τὰ πράγματα ποτὲ μὲν καταφάσκομεν, οἷον Θέων διαλέγεται ἔστι δὲ μὴ μόνον καταφάσκοντας ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀποφάσκοντας ἐκφέρειν τὰς διηγήσεις, καταφάσκοντας μέν, ὡς ἔφαμεν τὸν Θουκυδίδην τὴν διήγησιν ἐξενηνοχέναι ἀποφάσκοντας δέ, οἷον οὔτε Θηβαίων ἄνδρες ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σὺν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας, οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων ξυμμαχίδα, οὔτε τὰς πύλας ἀνέῳξαν Ναυκλείδης τε καὶ οἱ μετʼ αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὕτω μέχρι τέλους. ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλος τρόπος ἀσύνδετος καλούμενος, ὅταν τοὺς συνδέοντας τὴν φράσιν συνδέσμους παραλείπωμεν, οἷον Θηβαίων ἄνδρες ὀλίγῳ πλείους τριακοσίων εἰσῆλθον περὶ πρῶτον ὕπνον σύν ὅπλοις εἰς Πλάταιαν τῆς Βοιωτίας, οὖσαν Ἀθηναίων συμμαχίδα· ἀνέῳξαν αὐτοῖς τὰς πύλας Ναυκλείδης τε καὶ οἱ μετʼ αὐτοῦ, ἔθεντο εἰς τὴν ἀγορὰν τὰ ὅπλα. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. καὶ παρὰ Δημοσθένει Ἀμφίπολιν, Πύδναν, Ποτίδαιαν, Ἁλόννησον, οὐδενὸς τούτων μέμνημαι. ἔτι καὶ πάλιν· ἀλλʼ ἐφʼ Ἑλλήσποντον οἴχεται, πρότερον ἧκεν ἐπʼ Ἀμβρακίαν, Ἦλιν ἔχει, τηλικαύτην πόλιν ἐν Πελοποννήσῳ· Μεγάροις ἐπεβούλευσε πρῴην. ἔστι δὲ καὶ τούτους ἀλλήλοις ἐπιπλέκειν τοὺς τρόπους καὶ μικτὸν ἐκ δυοῖν ἢ πλειόνων ποιεῖν, ὡς τοῦ διηγήματος τὰ μὲν ἀπαγγεῖλαι κατὰ τὸν τοῦ ἀποφαινομένου τρόπον, τὰ δὲ ἀσυνδέτως, τὰ δὲ ὅπως ἄν τις βούλοιτο ποικίλλων τὴν φράσιν.
verses.heading: The modes of delivery, on one sentence of Thucydides

verses.text:
To add a comment to a narrative is to append a maxim to each part of the narrative. Such a thing suits neither history nor a political speech, but is rather adapted to the theatre and the stage. Therefore it occurs most abundantly among poets of that kind, as in Menander in many places, and at the beginning of both the Dardanus and the Recruiter: the son of a poor man, brought up with no resources, was ashamed to see his father possessing little; for having been well educated, he straightway rendered a fine fruit. For the last line is added superfluously, merely hunting the applause of the spectators.

When, however, one mixes such maxims in continuously and they pass unnoticed, the narrative becomes in a way charming — as in Herodotus in the first book. For speaking about human life, that it is not stable but has many changes in itself, and then reckoning up of how many days a human life consists, namely seventy years, he adds: of all these days not one brings on anything at all like another. Then he adds the comment in this manner: thus, Croesus, man is wholly chance. So too Gyges says to Candaules: master, what unsound proposal is this, bidding me look upon my mistress naked? For a woman puts off her modesty along with her tunic.

And indeed we might find the same among the orators, not least in the most political of writers, Demosthenes, and in his most political speeches. For in the second Olynthiac, narrating about Philip that he keeps about him mimes of ridiculous things and composers of shameful songs — men whom the city of the Athenians expelled as being utterly licentious — and that Philip, being such a man, naturally escapes the notice of everyone through his success in war, he afterwards adds the comment: for successes are terribly apt to conceal and overshadow such disgraces.

It is possible also, conversely, to set a sententious statement first and then narrate, just as we noted in the case of the fable — as in Menander, in The Worthy Heiress: is sleeplessness the most talkative of all things? and then the narrative follows: it has roused me and brought me out here to tell my whole life from the beginning.
verses.greek: Ἐπιφωνεῖν δὲ διηγήσει ἐστὶ τὸ καθʼ ἕκαστον μέρος τῆς διηγήσεως γνώμην ἐπιλέγειν, τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον οὔθʼ ἱστορίᾳ πρέπον ἐστὶν οὔτε πολιτικῷ λόγῳ, θεάτρῳ δὲ καὶ σκηνῇ μᾶλλον ἐπιτήδειον. διὸ καὶ παρὰ τοῖς τοιούτοις ποιηταῖς ἐπιπλεῖστόν ἐστιν, ὡς παρὰ Μενάνδρῳ πολλαχοῦ μὲν ἀλλαχόθι, καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ δὲ τοῦ τε Δαρδάνου καὶ τοῦ ξενολόγου, ἀνδρὸς πένητος υἱός, ἐκτεθραμμένος οὐκ ἐξ ὑπαρχόντων, ὁρῶν ᾐσχύνετο τὸν πατέρα μίκρʼ ἔχοντα· παιδευθεὶς γὰρ εὖ τὸν καρπὸν εὐθὺς ἀπεδίδου καλόν. ὁ γὰρ τελευταῖος στίχος ἐκ περιττοῦ πρόσκειται θηρώμενος μόνον τὸν παρὰ τῶν θεατῶν ἔπαινον. ὅταν μέντοι συνεχῶς ἐγκαταμιγνύῃ τις, καὶ λανθάνῃ ταῦτα τὰ γνωμικά, ἐπιχαρίς πως ἡ διήγησις γίνεται, ὡς παρὰ Ἡροδότῳ ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ· λέγων γὰρ περὶ τοῦ ἀνθρωπείου βίου, ὡς οὐκ ἔστι σταθερὸς ἀλλὰ πολλὰς ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἔχει τὰς μεταβολάς, ἔπειτα ἐξαριθμησάμενος ὅσων ἡμερῶν ἐστιν ἀνθρωπίνη ζωή, ὡς ἑβδομήκοντα ἔτη, ἐπιφέρει· τούτων τῶν ἁπασέων ἡμερέων ἡ ἑτέρη αὐτέων τῇ ἑτέρῃ ἡμέρῃ τὸ παράπαν οὐ δὲν ὅμοιον εἰσάγει πρῆγμα, εἶτα ἐπιφωνεῖ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον οὕτως, ὦ Κροῖσε, πᾶς ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος συμφορή. ὡς καὶ ὁ Γύγης πρὸς τὸν Κανδαύλην λέγει δέσποτα, τίνα λόγον ἔχεις οὐχ ὑγιέα, κελεύων δέσποιναν τὴν ἐμὴν θεήσασθαι γυμνήν; ἅμα δὲ χιτῶνι ἐκδυομένῳ συνεκδύεται καὶ τὴν αἰδὼ γυνή. καὶ μὴν καὶ παρὰ τοῖς ῥήτορσιν εὕροιμεν ἄν, οὐχʼ ἥκιστα καὶ παρὰ τῷ πολιτικωτάτῳ Δημοσθένει καὶ ἐν τοῖς πολιτικωτάτοις αὐτοῦ λόγοις· ἐν γὰρ τῷ δευτέρῳ τῶν Ὀλυνθιακῶν διηγούμενος περὶ τοῦ Φιλίππου, ὅτι περὶ αὑτὸν ἔχει μίμους γελοίων καὶ ποιητὰς αἰσχρῶν ἀσμάτων, καὶ οὕς γε ἡ πόλις Ἀθηναίων ἐξέβαλεν ὡς ἀσελγεστάτους ὄντας, καὶ ὅτι τοιοῦτος ὢν Φίλιππος εἰκότως λανθάνει πάντας ἀνθρώπους τῷ κατορθοῦν ἐν τοῖς πολέμοις, μετὰ ταῦτα ἐπιφωνεῖ· αἱ γὰρ εὐπραξίαι δειναὶ συγκρύψαι καὶ συσκιάσαι τὰ τοιαῦτα ὀνείδη. ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἀνάπαλιν προθέντα γνωμικὸν λόγον διηγήσασθαι, καθάπερ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ μύθου παρεσημειωσάμεθα, οἷον καὶ παρὰ Μενάνδρῳ ἐν τῇ χρηστῇ ἐπικλήρῳ, ἆρ᾽ ἐστὶ πάντων ἀγρυπνία λαλίστατον; εἶτα ἐξῆς τὸ διήγημα. ἐμὲ γοῦν ἀναστήσασα δευρὶ προάγεται λαλεῖν ἀπʼ ἀρχῆς πάντα τὸν ἐμαυτοῦ βίον.
verses.heading: Adding a comment to the narrative

verses.text: To interweave one narrative with another is when we undertake to narrate two or even more narratives at once. The school of Isocrates practised this especially, and Isocrates himself in the Panegyricus, thus: there came the children of Heracles, and a little before them Adrastus the son of Talaus, king of Argos, the latter having met with misfortune from the expedition against Thebes — and so on. And again: for while Greece was still lowly, there came into our land the Thracians with Eumolpus the son of Poseidon, and the Scythians with the Amazons, the daughters of Ares, not at the same time — and so on.
verses.greek: Διήγησιν δὲ διηγήσει συμπλέκειν ἐστίν, ὅταν δύο διηγήσεις ἢ καὶ πλείους ἅμα διηγεῖσθαι ἐπιχειρῶμεν, τοῦτο δὲ μάλα ἐπετήδευσαν οἱ ἀπὸ Ἰσοκράτους καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰσοκράτης ἐν τῷ πανηγυρικῷ οὕτως· ἦλθον οἵ θ᾿ Ἡρακλέους παῖδες, καὶ μικρὸν πρὸ τούτων Ἄδραστος ὁ Ταλαοῦ, βασιλεύς ὢν Ἄργους, οὗτος μὲν ἐκ τῆς στρατείας τῆς ἐπὶ Θήβας δεδυστυχηκώς καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς· καὶ πάλιν· ἔτι γὰρ ταπεινῆς οὔσης τῆς Ἑλλάδος ἦλθον εἰς τὴν χώραν ἡμῶν Θρᾷκες μὲν μετὰ Εὐμόλπου τοῦ Ποσειδῶνος, Σκύθαι δὲ μετὰ Ἀμαζόνων, τῶν Ἄρεως θυγατέρων, οὐ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον καὶ τὰ ἐξῆς.
verses.heading: Interweaving two narratives

verses.text:
Concerning refutation and confirmation we have said that the same topics are useful as for the fables; but in narratives the topics from falsehood and from impossibility are fitting as well. This is what Thucydides does in refuting the view that Hipparchus was killed by Harmodius and Aristogeiton and their party while he was tyrant; and Herodotus, in opposing those who declare that Cambyses was Egyptian on his mother's side.

It is not always possible to argue from all the topics in narratives; but whenever it can be done, we shall use this order. First from obscurity, in all the ways we spoke of concerning clarity. Second we shall argue from impossibility, showing that it was impossible for the matter to have happened as the writer says — either because it is not in the nature of things to happen at all, or because the events recorded do not fall in the same period of time. So, for instance, against those who say that Heracles killed Busiris; for according to Hesiod, Busiris is older than Heracles by eleven generations. And in general, for many such cases we shall have starting points for our arguments from the refutations of Arion.

Next, even if we grant that the matter is possible, it must be said that it is implausible; and if it is plausible, we shall consider whether it is false; and if it appears true, we shall next inquire whether something is deficient or excessive; and then that the writer contradicts himself in the course of the narrative. Besides these, we shall find fault with the order of the headings, if it has not been arranged fittingly. And if all these things have been suitably disposed, it must nevertheless be shown to be unseemly and unprofitable. For there are matters which ought not to have been done, and which, once done, it is better to pass over in silence — as if someone, having said that Locrian Ajax committed such impieties against Athena as are reported, should then suppose that he suffered no harm either at sea or at home, but died in old age in prosperity.

We shall readily be well supplied with more arguments if, in arguing from each of the topics handed on, we use also the so-called elements out of which every action is constituted: these are the ones we mentioned before — person, act, place, time, manner, and cause.
verses.greek: Περὶ δὲ ἀνασκευῆς καὶ κατασκευῆς εἴπομεν ὅτι οἱ αὐτοὶ τόποι χρήσιμοι, οἵπερ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς μύθους, ἐν δὲ τοῖς διηγήμασι καὶ οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ ψευδοῦς καὶ ἀδυνάτου τόποι ἁρμόττουσιν, ὅπερ ποιεῖ Θουκυδίδης μὲν ἀνασκευάζων τὸ μὴ τύραννον ὄντα Ἵππαρχον ὑπὸ τῶν περὶ τὸν Ἁρμόδιον καὶ Ἀριστογείτονα ἀναιρεθῆναι, Ἡρόδοτος δὲ ἐναντιούμενος τοῖς ἀποφαινομένοις Αἰγύπτιον εἶναι μητρόθεν τὸν Καμβύσην. οὐκ ἀεὶ μὲν οὖν οἷόν τε ἐκ πάντων τῶν τόπων ἐν τοῖς διηγήμασιν ἐπιχειρεῖν, ἐὰν δέ ποτε ἐγγένηται, ταύτῃ τῇ τάξει χρησόμεθα, πρῶτον μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀσαφοῦς, καθʼ ὅσους τρόπους περὶ σαφηνείας εἴπομεν, δεύτερον δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀδυνάτου ἐπιχειρήσομεν, δεικνύντες ὅτι ἀδύνατον τὸ πρᾶγμα οὕτω γενέσθαι, ὥς φησιν ὁ συγγραφεὺς ἤτοι διὰ τὸ μηδʼ ὅλως πεφυκέναι γίνεσθαι, ἢ διὰ τὸ μὴ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον εἶναι τὰ ἱστορούμενα, οἷον πρὸς τοὺς λέγοντας, ὅτι Ἡρακλῆς ἀπέκτεινε Βούσιριν· κατὰ γὰρ Ἡσίοδον πρεσβύτερος Ἡρακλέους ἐστὶν ὁ Βούσιρις ἕνδεκα γενεαῖς. καὶ ὅλως πρὸς τὰ πολλὰ τῶν τοιούτων ἀφορμὰς ἕξομεν λόγων ἐκ τῶν Ἀρίωνος ἐλέγχων. ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ εἰ δυνατὸν ὑποθοίμεθα τὸ πρᾶγμα, λεκτέον ὅτι ἀπίθανόν ἐστιν εἰ δὲ καὶ πιθανόν ἐστι, σκεψόμεθα εἰ ψευδές ἐστιν· εἰ δὲ ἀληθὲς φανείη, ἑξῆς ζητήσομεν, εἰ ἐλλείπει τι ἢ πλεονάζει· ἔπειτα δὲ ὅτι μάχεται κατὰ τὴν διήγησιν αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ ὁ συγγραφεύς· πρὸς δὲ τούτοις μεμψόμεθα καὶ τὴν τάξιν τῶν κεφαλαίων, εἰ μὴ προσηκόντως εἴη γεγενημένη. εἰ δὲ ταῦτα πάντα κατὰ τρόπον εἴη διατεθειμένα, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἀπρεπές τε καὶ ἀσύμφορον δεικτέον ἔστι γὰρ τῶν πραγμάτων ἃ πραχθῆναι μὲν οὐκ ἐχρῆν, φθάσαντα δὲ πραχθῆναι σιωπᾶσθαι συμφέρει, οἶον εἴ τις τὸν Λοκρὸν Αἴαντα τοιαῦτα εἰπὼν εἰς τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν ἀσεβῆσαι οἶα λέγεται, ἔπειτα ὑπόθοιτο μήτε ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ μήτε οἴκοι κακόν τι αὐτὸν πεπονθότα, ἐν γήρᾳ μετʼ εὐδαιμονίας τετελευτηκέναι. ῥᾳδίως δὲ καὶ πλειόνων εὐπορήσομεν ἐπιχειρημάτων, ἐὰν καθʼ ἕκαστον τῶν παραδεδομένων τόπων ἐπιχειροῦντες χρώμεθα καὶ τοῖς καλουμένοις στοιχείοις, ἐξ ὧν ἅπασα πρᾶξις ὑφίσταται· ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα ἐξ ὧν προείπομεν, πρόσωπον, πρᾶγμα, τόπος, χρόνος, τρόπος, αἰτία.
verses.heading: Refutation and confirmation: the topics

verses.text:
For the sake of example, let our discussion be on a single topic, that of implausibility. If, then, we are refuting the narrative from implausibility, we shall proceed thus, showing that the person is implausible, and the act, and the place in which the act occurred, and likewise the time and the manner and the cause of the act.

Take the case of Medea. From the person: that it is implausible for a mother to do harm to her children. From the act: that it is not likely she cut their throats. From the place: that she would not have killed them in Corinth, where Jason, the children's father, was staying. From the time: that it is implausible at that particular time, when she herself had been humbled, cast out by her husband, a foreign woman, while Jason had acquired greater power by marrying Glauce, the daughter of Creon the king of those parts. From the manner: that she would have tried to escape notice, and would not have made away with them by the sword but by a drug — especially as she was a sorceress. From the cause: that it is implausible that she killed the children through anger against her husband; for the misfortune was not Jason's alone but common to her as well, and hers the more, inasmuch as women are somehow softer in the face of suffering.

In the same way we shall go over the other topics too, arguing according to the successive elements from whichever we can; and from the opposite topics we shall confirm.

These same topics are fitting also for mythical narratives, both those told by the poets and those told by the historians about gods and heroes, and further about creatures altered from their nature, such as some record concerning Pegasus and Erichthonius and the Chimaera and the Hippocentaurs and the like.

But not merely to refute such tales, but also to show the source from which such an account has slipped in, belongs to a more complete competence than most men possess. This is what Herodotus did in the second book, narrating about the doves — how they flew out of Egypt, and one came to Dodona and the other to the shrine of Ammon. Explaining the tale, he says that certain maidens from Egyptian Thebes were priestesses, one of whom was sold to Dodona and the other to the shrine of Ammon; and since they spoke in a foreign tongue and unintelligibly to the natives, an account prevailed that they were birds. Plato too, in the Phaedrus, not accepting the narrative about Oreithyia and Boreas, says that a blast of the north wind pushed Oreithyia down the rocks nearby while she was playing with Pharmaceia, and that thus it came to be said that she had been snatched away by Boreas.

And indeed Ephorus in the fourth book uses this manner: that Tityus was a ruler of Panopeus, a lawless and violent man; that Python was bestial in nature and nicknamed the Serpent; and that those who inhabited the place formerly called Phlegra and now named Pallene were savage men, temple-robbers and eaters of human flesh, the so-called Giants, whom Heracles is said to have subdued after taking Troy; and that, because Heracles and his men, being few, prevailed over the Giants, who were many and impious, the affair of the battle seemed to everyone to have been the work of gods. He resolves many other such tales as well, about Lycurgus and Minos and Rhadamanthus and Zeus and the Curetes and the other things told as myths in Crete.

Palaephatus the Peripatetic also has a whole book entitled On Incredible Things, in which he resolves such matters: for instance, that those first seen riding on horses were supposed to be Centaurs; that Diomedes the Thracian, having exhausted his substance on horse-breeding, was said to have been destroyed by his own horses; and by the same account Actaeon by his dogs; and that Medea, by dyeing the grey hairs on people's heads and making them black, got the reputation of cutting old men up into a cauldron and making them young; and things like these.
verses.greek: Παραδείγματος δὲ ἕνεκα ὁ λόγος ἡμῖν ἔστω ἐφʼ ἑνὸς τόπου τοῦ ἀπιθάνου. ἐὰν τοίνυν ἀνασκευάζωμεν τὴν διήγησιν ἐκ τοῦ ἀπιθάνου, οὕτως ἐπεξελευσόμεθα, δεικνύντες ὅτι καὶ τὸ πρόσωπον ἀπίθανόν ἐστι καὶ τὸ πραχθὲν καὶ ὁ τόπος, ἐν ᾧ ἡ πρᾶξις, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ χρόνος καὶ ὁ τρόπος καὶ ἡ αἰτία τῆς πράξεως, οἷον ἐπὶ τῆς Μηδείας ἐκ μὲν τοῦ προσώπου, ὅτι ἀπίθανόν ἐστι μητέρα κακῶς ποιῆσαι τέκνα, ἐκ δὲ τῆς πράξεως, ὅτι οὐκ εἰκός ἐστιν ἀποσφάξαι· ἐκ δὲ τοῦ τόπου, ὅτι οὐκ ἄν ἀπέκτεινεν ἐν Κορίνθῳ, ὅπου διέτριβεν Ἰάσων ὁ τῶν παίδων πατήρ· ἐκ δὲ τοῦ χρόνου, ὅτι ἀπίθανόν ἐστιν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ χρόνῳ, ἐν αὐτὴ μὲν ἐτεταπείνωτο τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἐκπεσοῦσα ξένη γυνή, ὁ δὲ Ἰάσων μείζω δύναμιν προσειλήφει γήμας Γλαύκην τὴν Κρέοντος τοῦ βασιλέως τῶν τόπων θυγατέρα· ἐκ δὲ τοῦ τρόπου, ὅτι ἐπειράθη ἂν λαθεῖν καὶ οὐκ ἄν ξίφει διεχρήσατο, ἀλλὰ φαρμάκῳ ἄλλως τε καὶ φαρμακὶς οὖσα· ἐκ δὲ τῆς αἰτίας, ὅτι ἀπίθανόν ἐστι διʼ ὀργὴν τὴν πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα ἀπεκτονέναι τὰ τέκνα· οὐ γὰρ ἴδιον τοῦ Ἰάσονος, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτῆς κοινὸν ἐγένετο τὸ ἀτύχημα, καὶ μᾶλλον αὐτῆς, ὅσῳ μαλακώτεραί πως αἱ γυναῖκες πρὸς τὰ πάθη. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων τόπων ἐφοδεύσομεν κατὰ τὰ ἑξῆς στοιχεῖα ἐπιχειροῦντες ἐξ ὧν ἂν δυνατὸν ᾖ, ἐκ δὲ τῶν ἐναντίων τόπων κατασκευάσομεν. οἱ δ᾿ αὐτοὶ οὗτοι ἁρμόττουσι καὶ πρὸς τὰς μυθικὰς διηγήσεις τάς τε ὑπὸ τῶν ποιητῶν καὶ τὰς ὑπὸ τῶν ἱστορικῶν λεγομένας περί τε θεῶν καὶ ἡρώων, ἔτι τε καὶ τῶν ἐξηλλαγμένων κατὰ φύσιν, οἷά τινες ἱστοροῦσι περὶ Πηγάσου καὶ Ἐριχθονίου καὶ Χιμαίρας καὶ Ἱπποκενταύρων καὶ τῶν παραπλησίων. τὸ δὲ μὴ μόνον ἀνασκευάζειν τὰς τοιαύτας μυθολογίας, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅθεν παρερρύηκεν ὁ τοιοῦτος λόγος ἀποφαίνειν τελεωτέρας ἐστὶν ἕξεως ἢ κατὰ τοὺς πολλούς, ὅπερ πεποίηκεν Ἡρόδοτος μὲν ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ περὶ τῶν πελειάδων διηγούμενος, ὡς ἐξέπτησαν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου, καὶ ἡ μὲν εἰς Δωδώνην, ἡ δὲ εἰς Ἄμμωνος ἀφίκετο, ἐξηγούμενός τε τὸ μυθολόγημά φησιν, ὅτι παρθένοι τινὲς ἐκ Θηβῶν τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ἦσαν ἱέρειαι, ὧν ἡ μὲν εἰς Δωδώνην ἐπράθη, ἡ δὲ εἰς Ἄμμωνος, καὶ ἐπειδὴ βαρβαριστὶ ἐφθέγγοντο καὶ ἀξυνέτως τοῖς ἐπιχωρίοις, λόγος κατέσχεν ὡς ὄρνιθες ἦσαν. Πλάτων δὲ ἐν τῷ Φαίδρῳ τὸ περὶ τῆς Ὠρειθυίας καὶ τοῦ Βορέου διήγημα οὐκ ἀποδεχόμενός φησι τὴν Ὠρείθυιαν πνεῦμα βορέου κατὰ τῶν πλησίον πετρῶν σὺν Φαρμακείᾳ παίζουσαν ὦσαι, καὶ οὕτω δὴ λεχθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ βορέου ἀνάρπαστον γεγονέναι. καὶ μέντοι καὶ Ἔφορος ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ χρῆται τούτῳ τῷ τρόπῳ, ὅτι ἄρα Τιτυὸς μὲν ἦν Πανοπέως δυνάστης, ἀνὴρ παράνομος καὶ βίαιος, Πύθων δὲ θηριώδης τὴν φύσιν, δράκων ἐπικαλούμενος, οἱ δὲ περὶ τὴν πάλαι μὲν Φλέγραν, νῦν δὲ Παλλήνην ὀνομαζομένην κατοικοῦντες ἦσαν ἄνθρωποι ὠμοὶ καὶ ἱερόσυλοι καὶ ἀνθρωποφάγοι, οἱ καλούμενοι Γίγαντες, οὓς Ἡρακλῆς λέγεται χειρώσασθαι τὴν Τροίαν ἑλών, καὶ διὰ τὸ κρατῆσαι τοὺς περὶ τὸν Ἡρακλέα ὀλίγους ὄντας τῶν Γιγάντων πολλῶν ὄντων καὶ ἀσεβῶν θεῶν ἔργον ἅπασιν ἐδόκει γεγονέναι τὸ περὶ τὴν μάχην, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα τοιαῦτα ἐπιλύεται περὶ τοῦ Λυκούργου καὶ Μίνωος καὶ Ῥαδαμάνθυος καὶ Διὸς καὶ κουρήτων καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν ἐν τῇ Κρήτῃ μυθολογουμένων καὶ Παλαιφάτῳ τῷ Περιπατητικῷ ἐστιν ὅλον βιβλίον περὶ τῶν ἀπίστων ἐπιγραφόμενον, ἐν τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐπιλύεται, οἷον ὅτι Κένταυροι μὲν ὑπελήφθησαν οἱ πρῶτοι ἐπὶ ἵπποις ὀχούμενοι ὀφθέντες, Διομήδης δὲ Θρᾷξ ἐς ἱπποτροφίαν ἐξαναλωθεὶς ἐλέχθη ὑπὸ τῶν αὑτοῦ ἵππων ἀπολωλέναι, κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον καὶ Ἀκταίων ὑπὸ τῶν κυνῶν, ἡ δὲ Μήδεια βάπτουσα τὰς ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων πολιὰς καὶ μελαίνας ποιοῦσα ἐφημίσθη τοὺς γέροντας εἰς λέβητα κατακόπτουσα νέους ποιεῖν, καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια τούτοις.
verses.heading: A worked refutation (Medea), and rationalizing the myths

verses.text: So much, then, for the manners of the exercise; and note that it is possible to train by these same manners in the fables as well.
verses.greek: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τῶν τρόπων τῆς γυμνασίας τοσαῦτα, καὶ ὅτι κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς δυνατόν ἐστι γυμνάσασθαι κἀν τοῖς μύθοις.
verses.heading: Closing

verses.text: A chreia is a concise statement or action, aptly attributed to a definite person or to something corresponding to a person. Closely related to it are the maxim and the reminiscence: for every concise maxim attributed to a person makes a chreia, and the reminiscence too is an action or a saying useful for life. The maxim differs from the chreia in these four respects: that the chreia is always attributed to a person, the maxim not always; that the chreia sometimes states a general truth and sometimes a particular one, whereas the maxim states only the general; further, that the chreia sometimes makes a joke and has nothing useful for life in it, whereas the maxim always concerns what is useful in life; and fourth, that the chreia is an action or a saying, while the maxim is a saying only. The reminiscence is marked off from the chreia in these two respects: the chreia is concise, whereas the reminiscence is sometimes extended; and the chreia is attributed to particular persons, whereas the reminiscence is remembered also for its own sake. It is called chreia par excellence because, more than the others, it is useful for many purposes in life — just as, though there are many poets, we are accustomed to call Homer alone “the Poet” par excellence.
verses.greek: Χρεία ἐστὶ σύντομος ἀπόφασις ἢ πρᾶξις μετ᾿ εὐστοχίας ἀναφερομένη εἴς τι ὡρισμένον πρόσωπον ἢ ἀναλογοῦν προσώπῳ, παράκειται δὲ αὐτῇ γνώμη καὶ ἀπομνημόνευμα· πᾶσα γὰρ γνώμη σύντομος εἰς πρόσωπον ἀναφερομένη χρείαν ποιεῖ. καὶ τὸ ἀπομνημόνευμα δὲ πρᾶξίς ἐστιν ἢ λόγος βιωφελής. διαφέρει δὲ ἡ μὲν γνώμη τῆς χρείας τέτρασι τοῖσδε, τῷ τὴν μὲν χρείαν πάντως ἀναφέρεσθαι εἰς πρόσωπον, τὴν δὲ γνώμην οὐ πάντως, καὶ τῷ ποτὲ μὲν τὸ καθόλου, ποτὲ δὲ τὸ ἐπὶ μέρους ἀποφαίνεσθαι τὴν χρείαν, τὴν δὲ γνώμην καθόλου μόνον· ἔτι δὲ τῷ χαριεντίζεσθαι τὴν χρείαν ἐνίοτε μηδὲν ἔχουσαν βιωφελές, τὴν δὲ γνώμην ἀεὶ περὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ βίῳ χρησίμων εἶναι· τέταρτον ὅτι ἡ μὲν χρεία πρᾶξις ἢ λόγος ὑπάρχει, ἡ δὲ γνώμη λόγος ἐστὶ μόνον. τὸ δὲ ἀπομνημόνευμα δυσὶ τοῖσδε κεχώρισται τῆς χρείας· ἡ μὲν γὰρ σύντομος, τὸ δὲ ἀπομνημόνευμα ἕσθ᾿ ὅτε ἐπεκτείνεται, καὶ ἡ μὲν ἀναφέρεται εἴς τινα πρόσωπα, τὸ δὲ ἀπομνημόνευμα καὶ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸ μνημονεύεται. εἴρηται δὲ χρεία κατ᾿ ἐξοχήν, ὅτι μᾶλλον τῶν ἄλλων πρὸς πολλὰ χρειώδης ἐστὶ τῷ βίῳ, καθάπερ καὶ Ὅμηρον πολλῶν ὄντων ποιητῶν κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν τοῦτον μόνον καλεῖν εἰώθαμεν ποιητήν.
verses.heading: Definition, and why it is so called

verses.text: Of the chreia there are three highest classes: some are verbal, some active, and some mixed. Verbal are those that have their force through words, without an action — for example, Diogenes the philosopher, when someone asked him how he might become famous, answered, “By caring as little as possible about fame.” Of the verbal there are two species, the declarative and the responsive. Of the declarative, some are by voluntary statement — for example, Isocrates the sophist used to say that gifted students are children of gods; others arise out of a circumstance — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a rich but uneducated youth, said, “This fellow is filth plated with silver”; for Diogenes did not simply make the statement, but out of what he saw. Again, of the responsive there are four species: that by [yes-or-no] question, that by inquiry, that by question with a reason attached, and the one called responsive by the same name as its class. A question differs from an inquiry in that to a question one need only assent or deny — nod or shake the head, or answer with a yes or a no — whereas an inquiry demands a longer answer. An example by question: Pittacus of Mytilene, asked whether a man doing something wicked escapes the notice of the gods, said, “No — not even in intending it”; for what is added after the denial is superfluous, since the denial would have sufficed even if it were taken away. The inquiry type is like this: Theano the Pythagorean philosopher, asked by someone how soon after being with a man a woman may go down to the Thesmophorion pure, said, “After her own husband, at once; after another’s, never.” Those by question with a reason are such as contain, besides the answer to the question, some cause or advice or the like — for example, Socrates, asked whether the king of the Persians seemed to him happy, said, “I cannot say, since I do not even know how he stands in education.” Responsive [in the narrow sense] are those that come neither by question nor by inquiry, but where there is some remark to which the reply is made — for example, once when Diogenes was lunching in the marketplace and called him over to lunch, Plato said, “Diogenes, how charming your lack of affectation would be, if it were not affected”; for Diogenes was not asking Plato about anything, nor is Plato inquiring of him, but simply invites him to lunch, which belongs to neither kind. Besides these there is another species falling among the verbal chreiai, called double. A double chreia is one containing the statements of two persons, either of which by itself, with one person, makes a chreia — for example, Alexander king of the Macedonians, standing over Diogenes as he slept, said, “A man who is a counsellor should not sleep the whole night through,” and Diogenes replied, “— one to whom the peoples are entrusted and who has so many cares”; for it would have been a chreia even so, without the reply added. Active are those that reveal some thought without speech. Of the active, some are agentive and some passive. Agentive are those that show some action — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a greedy boy, struck his tutor with his staff. Passive are those that signify something suffered — for example, Didymus the flute-player, convicted of adultery, was hanged by the part his name denotes. Mixed are those that share in both the verbal and the active but have their force in the active — for example, Pythagoras the philosopher, asked how long the life of men is, went up to his bedroom and looked out for a moment, showing by this its brevity. And again, when someone asked a Laconian where the Lacedaemonians have the boundaries of their land, he pointed to his spear.
verses.greek: Τῆς δὲ χρείας τὰ ἀνωτάτω γένη τρία αἱ μὲν γάρ εἰσι λογικαί, αἱ δὲ πρακτικαί, αἰ δὲ μικταί. λογικαὶ μέν εἰσιν αἰ χωρὶς πράξεως διὰ λόγων ἔχουσαι τὸ κῦρος, οἷον Διογένης ὁ φιλόσοφος ἐρωτηθεὶς ὑπό τινος, πῶς ἄν ἔνδοξος γένοιτο, ἀπεκρίνατο, ὅτι ἥκιστα δόξης φροντίζων τῶν δὲ λογικῶν εἴδη δύο, ἀποφαντικὸν καὶ ἀποκριτικόν· του δὲ ἀποφαντικοῦ αἱ μέν εἰσι καθʼ ἑκούσιον ἀπόφασιν, οἷον Ἰσοκράτης ὁ σοφιστὴς τοὺς εὐφυεῖς τῶν μαθητῶν θεῶν παῖδας ἔλεγεν εἶναι αἱ δὲ κατὰ περίστασιν, οἷον Διογένης ὁ Κυνικὸς φιλόσοφος ἰδὼν μειράκιον πλούσιον ἀπαίδευτον εἶπεν, οὗτός ἐστι ῥύπος περιηργυρωμένος· οὐ γὰρ ὁ Διογένης ἁπλῶς ἀπεφήνατο, ἀλλ᾿ ἐξ ὧν εἶδεν ἔτι καὶ τοῦ ἀποκριτικοῦ εἰσιν εἴδη τέσσαρα, τό τε κατ ἐρώτησιν, καὶ τὸ κατὰ πύσμα, καὶ τὸ κατ᾿ ἐρώτησιν αἰ τιῶδες, καὶ τὸ ὁμωνύμως τῷ γένει λεγόμενον ἀποκριτικόν. διαφέρει δὲ τοῦ πύσματος ἡ ἐρώτησις, ὅτι πρὸς μὲν τὴν ἐρώτησιν συγκαταθέσθαι δεῖ μόνον ἢ ἀρνήσασθαι, οἷον ἀνανεῦσαι ἢ κατανεῦσαι, ἢ διά γε τοῦ ναὶ ἢ οὒ ἀποκρίνασθαι, τὸ δὲ πύσμα μακροτέραν ἀπαιτεῖ τὴν ἀπόκρισιν· κατ᾿ ἐρώτησιν μὲν οὖν ἐστιν, οἷον Πιττακὸς ὁ Μιτυληναῖος ἐρωτηθείς, εἰ λανθάνει τις τοὺς θεοὺς φαῦλόν τι ποιῶν, εἶπεν, οὒ οὐδὲ διανοούμενος. μετὰ γὰρ τὴν ἀπόφασιν τὸ προστιθέμενον περισσόν ἐστιν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀφαιρεθέντος αὐτοῦ ἀπήρκει ἡ ἀπόφασις. ἡ δὲ πυσματικὴ τοιαύτη ἐστίν, οἷον Θεανὼ ἡ Πυθαγορικὴ φιλόσοφος ἐρωτηθεῖσα ὑπό τινος, ποσταία γυνὴ ἀπʼ ἀνδρὸς καθαρὰ εἰς τὸ θεσμοφορεῖον κάτεισιν, εἶπεν, ἀπὸ μὲν τοῦ ἰδίου παραχρῆμα, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου οὐδέποτε. αἰ δὲ κατʼ ἐρώτησιν αἰτιώδεις εἰσίν, ὅσαι χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τὴν ἐρώτησιν ἀποκρίσεως καὶ αἰτίαν τινὰ ἔχουσιν ἢ συμβουλὴν ἤ τι τοιοῦτον, οἷον Σωκράτης ἐρωτηθείς, εἰ εὐδαίμων αὐτῷ δοκεῖ ὁ τῶν Περσῶν βασιλεύς, οὐκ ἔχω λέγειν, εἶπε, μηδὲ γὰρ εἰδέναι πῶς ἔχει παιδείας. ἀποκριτικαὶ δέ εἰσιν αἱ μήτε κατ᾿ ἐρώτησιν, μήτε κατὰ πύσμα, λόγον δέ τινα ἔχουσαι, πρὸς ὅν ἐστιν ἡ ἀπόκρισις, οἷον Πλάτων ποτὲ Διογένους ἀριστῶντος ἐν ἀγορᾷ καὶ καλοῦντος αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄριστον, ὦ Διόγενες, εἶπεν, ὡς χάριεν ἂν ἦν σου τὸ ἄπλαστον, εἰ μὴ πλαστὸν ἦν οὔτε γὰρ Διογένης περί τινος ἠρώτα τὸν Πλάτωνα, οὔτε ὁ Πλάτων πυνθάνεται αὐτοῦ, ἀλλʼ ἁπλῶς πρὸς τὸ ἄριστον καλεῖ αὐτόν, ὅπερ ἐστὶ τῶν οὐδετέρων. ἔστι δὲ παρὰ ταῦτα καὶ ἄλλο εἶδος ἐμπῖπτον εἰς τὰς λογικὰς καλούμενον διπλοῦν, διπλῆ δέ ἐστι χρεία ἡ δύο προσώπων ἀποφάσεις ἔχουσα, ὧν καὶ ἡ ἑτέρα μεθ᾿ ἑνὸς προσώπου χρείαν ποιεῖ, οἷον Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ τῶν Μακεδόνων βασιλεὺς ἐπιστὰς Διογένει κοιμωμένῳ εἶπεν, οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα. καὶ ὁ Διογένης ἀπεκρίνατο, ᾧ λαοί τ᾿ ἐπιτετράφαται καὶ τόσσα μέμηλεν. ἦν γὰρ καὶ οὕτω χρεία μὴ προστιθεμένης τῆς ἀποκρίσεως. πρακτικαὶ δέ εἰσιν αἱ χωρὶς λόγου ἐμφαίνουσαι τινα νοῦν, τῶν δὲ πρακτικῶν αἱ μέν εἰσιν ἐνεργητικαί, αἱ δὲ παθητικαί, ἐνεργητικαὶ μὲν ὅσαι δηλοῦσί τινα ἐνέργειαν, οἷον Διογένης ὁ Κυνικὸς φιλόσοφος ἰδὼν ὀψοφάγον παῖδα τὸν παιδαγωγὸν τῇ βακτηρίᾳ ἔπαισε. παθητικαὶ δὲ αἱ πάθος τι σημαίνουσαι, οἷον Δίδυμος ὁ αὐλητὴς ἁλοὺς ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ ἐκ τοῦ ὀνόματος ἐκρεμάσθη. μικταὶ δέ εἰσιν ὅσαι τοῦ μὲν λογικοῦ καὶ τοῦ πρακτικοῦ κοινωνοῦσιν, ἐν δὲ τῷ πρακτικῷ τὸ κῦρος ἔχουσιν, οἷον Πυθαγόρας ὁ φιλόσοφος ἐρωτηθεὶς πόσος ἐστὶν ὁ τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίος, ἀναβὰς ἐπὶ τὸ δωμάτιον παρέκυψεν ὀλίγον, δηλῶν διὰ τούτου τὴν βραχύτητα. καὶ ἔτι Λάκων ἐρομένου τινὸς αὐτὸν ποῦ τοὺς ὅρους τῆς γῆς ἔχουσι Λακεδαιμόνιοι, ἔδειξε τὸ δόρυ.
verses.heading: The three classes

verses.text: These, then, are the species of chreiai. They are delivered: some as maxims, some with proof, some as a witticism, some by syllogism, some by enthymeme, some by example, some as a wish, some symbolically, some figuratively, some by ambiguity, some by a shift of subject, and some in combination, composed of whichever of the aforesaid modes. As a maxim: Bion the sophist used to say that the love of money is the mother-city of all vice. With proof: Isocrates the orator used to urge his pupils to honour their teachers above their parents, because parents are the cause of living only, but teachers of living well — for Isocrates brought out his statement together with its proof. As a witticism: Olympias, learning that her son Alexander was declaring himself the son of Zeus, said, “Will this fellow never stop slandering me to Hera?” By syllogism: Diogenes the philosopher, seeing a youth excessively adorned, said, “If it is for men, you are unlucky; if for women, you do wrong.” By enthymeme: when a companion, Apollodorus, said to Socrates the philosopher, “The Athenians have condemned you to death unjustly,” he laughed and said, “And would you have preferred justly?” — for we must supply the further thought that it is better to be condemned unjustly than justly, which seems to be left out of the chreia though it is conveyed by implication. By example: Alexander king of the Macedonians, urged by his friends to amass money, said, “But these things did not profit Croesus either.” As a wish: Damon the trainer, who was lame in the feet, when his shoes were stolen said, “May they fit the thief.” Symbolically: Alexander king of the Macedonians, asked by someone where he kept his treasures, said, “In these,” pointing to his friends. Figuratively: Plato the philosopher said that the shoots of virtue grow by sweat and toil. By ambiguity: when a boy was being introduced to Isocrates the orator and the one introducing him asked what the boy needed, he said, “A ΚΑΙΝΟΥ writing-tablet and a ΚΑΙΝΟΥ stylus” — for it is ambiguous whether he means a tablet and a mind (καὶ νοῦ), or a new (καινοῦ) tablet and a new stylus. It is by a shift of subject when the one answering transfers what is said and asked to something else — for example, when some men over their drinks were inquiring which was the better flute-player, Antigenidas or Satyrus, Pyrrhus king of the Epirotes said, “For my part, Polysperchon — as a general.” The combined mode plainly comes about in many ways: a witticism may be interwoven with a maxim, or an example with a symbol, or ambiguity with a shift of subject, or generally in as many other ways as a pairing can be made, with two or even more modes taken up into a single chreia — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a youth born of an adulterer throwing stones in the marketplace, said, “Stop, boy, or you may hit your father without knowing it”; for the saying is at once symbolic and witty.
verses.greek: Τὰ μὲν οὖν εἴδη τῶν χρειῶν ταῦτά ἐστι· προφέρονται δὲ αἱ μὲν γνωμολογικῶς, αἱ δὲ ἀποδεικτικῶς, αἱ δὲ κατὰ χαριεντισμόν, αἱ δὲ κατὰ συλλογισμόν, αἱ δὲ κατὰ ἐνθύμημα, αἱ δὲ κατὰ παράδειγμα, αἱ δὲ κατ᾿ εὐχήν, αἱ δὲ συμβολικῶς, αἱ δὲ τροπικῶς, αἱ δὲ κατὰ ἀμφιβολίαν, αἱ δὲ κατὰ μετάληψιν, αἱ δὲ συνεζευγμένως ἐξ οἵων δήποτε τῶν προειρημένων τρόπων συγκείμεναι. γνωμολογικῶς μὲν οἷον Βίων ὁ σοφιστὴς τὴν φιλαργυρίαν μητρόπολιν ἔλεγε πάσης κακίας εἶναι. ἀποδεικτικῶς δὲ οἷον Ἰσοκράτης ὁ ῥήτωρ παρῄνει τοῖς γνωρίμοις προτιμᾶν τῶν γονέων τοὺς διδασκάλους, ὅτι οἱ μὲν τοῦ ζῆν μόνον, οἱ δὲ διδάσκαλοι καὶ τοῦ καλῶς ζῆν αἴτιοι γεγόνασιν· τὴν γὰρ ἀπόφασιν αὐτοῦ Ἰσοκράτης μετὰ ἀποδείξεως ἐξενήνοχε. κατὰ χαριεντισμὸν δὲ οἷον Ὀλυμπιὰς πυθομένη τὸν υἱὸν Ἀλέξανδρον Διὸς αὐτὸν ἀποφαίνειν, οὐ παύσεται οὗτος, ἔφη, διαβάλλων με πρὸς τὴν Ἥραν; συλλογιστικῶς δὲ οἷον Διογένης ὁ φιλόσοφος ἰδὼν μειράκιον περισσῶς καλλωπιζόμενον εἶπεν· εἰ μὲν πρὸς ἄνδρας, ἀτυχεῖς, εἰ δὲ πρὸς γυναῖκας, ἀδικεῖς. ἐνθυμηματικῶς δὲ οἷον Σωκράτης ὁ φιλόσοφος Ἀπολλοδώρου τινὸς γνωρίμου λέγοντος αὐτῷ ἀδίκως σου θάνατον κατέγνωσαν Ἀθηναῖοι, γελάσας ἔφη, σὺ δὲ ἐβούλου δικαίως; προσενθυμεῖσθαι γὰρ ἡμὰς δεῖ, ὅτι ἄρα βέλτιον ἀδίκως ἢ δικαίως κατεγνῶσθαι, ὅπερ ἐν τῇ χρείᾳ δοκεῖ παραλελεῖφθαι δυνάμει δηλούμενον. κατὰ παράδειγμα δὲ οἷον Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ τῶν Μακεδόνων βασιλεύς παρακαλούμενος ὑπὸ τῶν φίλων συναγαγεῖν χρήματα, εἶπεν, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα οὐκ ὤνησεν οὐδὲ Κροῖσον. εὐκτικῶς δὲ οἷον Δάμων ὁ παιδοτρίβης χωλούς ἔχων τούς πόδας κλαπέντων αὐτοῦ τῶν ὑποδημάτων, ἔφη, εἴθε ἐναρμόσειε τῷ κλέπτῃ. συμβολικῶς δὲ οἷον Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ τῶν Μακεδόνων βασιλεύς ἐρωτηθεὶς ὑπό τινος, ποῦ ἔχει τοὺς θησαυρούς, ἐν τούτοις, ἔφη, δείξας τούς φίλους. τροπικῶς δὲ οἷον Πλάτων ὁ φιλόσοφος τοὺς τῆς ἀρετῆς κλῶνας ἔφη ἱδρῶτι καὶ πόνοις φύεσθαι. κατὰ ἀμφιβολίαν δέ, οἷον Ἰσοκράτης ὁ ῥήτωρ συνισταμένου αὐτῷ παιδίου καὶ ἐρωτῶντος τοῦ συνιστάντος, τίνος αὐτῷ δεῖ, εἶπε, πινακιδίου ΚΑΙΝΟΥ, καὶ γραφιδίου ΚΑΙΝΟΥ ἀμφιβαλλόμενον γάρ, πότερον νοῦ καὶ πινακιδίου λέγει ἢ πινακίδος καινῆς καὶ καινοῦ γραφιδίου. κατὰ μετάληψιν δέ ἐστιν, ὅταν τὸ λεγόμενον καὶ τὸ ἐρωτώμενον ἐπʼ ἄλλο τις ἀποκρινόμενος μεταλαμβάνῃ, οἷον Πύρρος ὁ τῶν Ἠπειρωτῶν βασιλεύς ζητούντων τινῶν παρὰ πότον, πότερος κρείττων αὐλητὴς Ἀντιγεννίδας ἢ Σάτυρος, ἐμοὶ μέν, εἶπε, στρατηγὸς Πολυσπέρχων. ὁ δὲ συνεζευγμένος τρόπος οὐκ ἄδηλός ἐστιν, ὅτι πολλαχῶς γίνεται· ἢ γὰρ γνωμικῷ χαριεντισμῷ συμπλακήσεται, ἢ παραδείγματι συμβολικῷ ἢ ἀμφιβολίᾳ καὶ μεταλήψει ἢ ἀπλῶς καθʼ ὅσους καὶ ἄλλους τρόπους δύναται συγγενέσθαι συζυγία, ἤτοι δυοῖν ἢ καὶ πλειόνων τρόπων εἰς μίαν χρείαν παραλαμβανομένων, οἷον Διογένης ὁ Κυνικὸς φιλόσοφος ἰδὼν μειράκιον ἐκ μοιχοῦ λίθους βάλλον εἰς ἀγοράν, παῦσαι, ἔφη, παιδίον, μὴ ἀγνοοῦν παίσῃς τὸν πατέρα. ἔχει γὰρ ἅμα καὶ συμβολικῶς καὶ χαριέντως ἡ ἀπόφασις.
verses.heading: The manners in which chreiai are delivered

verses.text: Students are exercised on chreiai by recitation, by inflection, by comment, and by objection; we also expand and compress the chreia, and besides these we refute and confirm it. Recitation is straightforward: when a chreia has been stated, we try to render it as clearly as we can, either in the very same words or in others. Inflection is various: we vary the persons in the chreia through the three numbers, and this not simply, but as one to one, two to two, and several to several; and again two to one, to two, and to several; and further several to one, to two, and to several. For when the chreia has been set out — that Isocrates the orator used to say the gifted are children of gods — we inflect it thus: one to one, “Isocrates the orator used to say that the gifted student is a child of gods”; two to two [in the dual], “The two Isocrateses, the two orators, used to say that the two gifted students are children of gods”; several to several, “The Isocrateses, the orators, used to say that the gifted students are children of gods.” It is clear from these how we shall inflect the other ways as well, for they are transferred into the five cases too. But since some chreiai are verbal, some active, and some mixed from both, and these again have further species, we shall try to teach the inflection of each of them by an example. The nominative presents no difficulty, for each of the chreiai is normally delivered in it. The genitive we shall inflect thus: if the chreia is verbal, we shall add to it “the saying was remembered,” or “a saying is recorded of him when he said.” The former is fitting to append after the whole chreia has been recited — for example, “Isocrates the orator saying that gifted students are children of gods, the saying was remembered”; the second is used in the middle of it, as the statement begins — for example, “Pittacus of Mytilene being asked whether a man doing something wicked escapes the notice of the gods, a saying is recorded of him when he said: not even in intending it.” “A saying is recorded” suits all the verbal chreiai better, except the one by voluntary statement; for that one takes “the saying was remembered.” If the chreia is active: should it be passive, one must add “what befell him was remembered”; should it be agentive, “what was done was remembered”; and similarly with the mixed. Each of these is to be added at the end of the chreia — for example, “Didymus the flute-player being convicted of adultery and hanged by the part his name denotes, what befell him was remembered”; and “Diogenes the Cynic philosopher seeing a greedy boy and striking his tutor with his staff, what was done was remembered.” To the dative, in every chreia except the passive, we shall add “it seemed good,” or “it appeared,” or “it occurred,” or “it came to him,” or something of the sort — for example, “To Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth, it seemed good to say: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” In the passive we shall add “it happened” — for example, “To Didymus the flute-player, convicted of adultery, it happened that he was hanged by the part his name denotes.” To the accusative we shall add, generally in every chreia, “they say” or “it is said” — for example, “Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth, they say (or, it is said) said: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” The vocative is clear: we shall address our words to the person as though he were present, to whom the chreia is attributed — for example, “Diogenes, Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth you said: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” To comment is to approve what has been said in the chreia, aptly and concisely: either that it is true, or that it is noble, or that it is advantageous, or that other men of proven worth held this same view. For example, Euripides the poet said that the mind of each of us is a god. We shall comment from truth thus: “for the mind is indeed a god to each man, urging us on to what is advantageous and holding us back from what does harm.” From the noble thus: “for it is a noble thing that each man should think the god to be not in gold and silver but in himself.” From the advantageous thus: “so that we may not, supposing that what punishes lies far off, have great readiness to do wrong.” From the testimony of the renowned, when we say that a sage, or a lawgiver, or a poet, or some other famous man is of one mind with what was said: for the chreia before us we shall say, “Such is the mind of men upon the earth as the father of men and gods brings on the day.” We object to chreiai from the contraries — as against Isocrates, when he said that teachers are to be honoured above fathers, since fathers furnished us living but teachers living well: for in objecting we say that there could be no living well, had not fathers first furnished the living. One must know that it is not possible to object to every chreia, since many are expressed well and blamelessly — just as it is not possible to praise them all, since with some the absurdity strikes one at once. We expand the chreia whenever we lengthen the questions and answers in it, and any action or experience contained in it; we compress by doing the opposite. A concise chreia, for example: “Epaminondas, dying childless, said to his friends…” — and we need more besides for it. (†) [Refutation may be drawn] from impossibility, as we might say against Isocrates that it is not possible for men to be born of gods, not even if they are gifted; from implausibility, that it is not likely that Antisthenes, an Athenian, having come from Athens to Lacedaemon, should say that he was passing from the women’s quarters into the men’s; from falsehood, that Bion did not speak truly in saying that the love of money is the mother-city of vice, for folly is more so; from the disadvantageous, that Simonides gives harmful advice in urging us to play in life and to be serious about nothing at all; from uselessness, as when what was said should appear of no benefit at all for life; from shamefulness, whenever we show the chreia to be shameful and open to reproach — for example, a man of Sybaris, seeing the Lacedaemonians living laboriously, said he did not wonder that in their wars they do not shrink from dying, since death is better than such a life; for he made his statement in a thoroughly soft manner, and not after a manly fashion. From these topics, then, one must refute; and one must argue against each part of the chreia, beginning from the first, from as many topics as prove possible — for let it not escape us that it is not possible in every chreia to argue from them all.
verses.greek: Γυμνάζονται δὲ κατὰ τὰς χρείας τῇ ἀπαγγελίᾳ τῇ κλίσει τῇ ἐπιφωνήσει τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ, ἐπεκτείνομέν τε καὶ συστέλλομεν τὴν χρείαν, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις ἀνασκευάζομεν καὶ κατασκευάζομεν. καὶ ἡ μὲν ἀπαγγελία φανερά ἐστι ῥηθεῖσαν γὰρ χρείαν πειρώμεθα κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν αὐτοῖς ὀνόμασιν ἢ καὶ ἑτέροις σαφέστατα ἑρμηνεῦσαι. ἡ δὲ κλίσις ἐστὶ ποικίλη· τὰ γὰρ ἐν τῇ χρεία πρόσωπα εἰς τοὺς τρεῖς ἀριθμούς ἐναλλάττομεν, καὶ τοῦτο οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλʼ οἷον ἑνὸς πρὸς ἔνα καὶ δύο πρὸς δύο καὶ πλείους πρὸς πλείους, καὶ πάλιν δυοῖν πρὸς ἕνα καὶ πρὸς δύο, καὶ πρὸς πλείους, ἔτι δὲ πλειόνων πρὸς ἕνα καὶ πρὸς δύο καὶ πρὸς πλείους. προκειμένης γὰρ χρείας, ὅτι Ἰσοκράτης ὁ ῥήτωρ τούς εὐφυέας τῶν θεῶν παῖδας ἔλεγεν εἶναι, οὕτω κλίνομεν ἑνὸς μὲν πρὸς ἔνα, οἷον Ἰσοκράτης ὁ ῥήτωρ τὸν εὐφυέα τῶν μαθητῶν θεῶν παῖδα ἔλεγεν εἶναι δυοῖν δὲ πρὸς δύο, Ἰσοκράτεε τώ ῥήτορε τὼ εὐφυέε τῶν μαθητῶν θεῶν παῖδε ἐλεγέτην εἶναι· πλειόνων δὲ πρὸς πλείους, Ἰσοκράτεις οἱ ῥήτορες τοὺς εὐφυεῖς τῶν μαθητῶν θεῶν παῖδας ἔλεγον εἶναι. φανερὸν δὲ ἐκ τούτων, πῶς καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους τρόπους κλινοῦμεν· μεταλαμβάνονται γὰρ καὶ εἰς τὰς πέντε πτώσεις. ἀλλʼ ἐπεὶ τῶν χρειῶν αἱ μέν εἰσι λογικαί, αἱ δὲ πρακτικαί, αἱ δὲ ἐξ ἀμφοῖν τούτοιν μικταί, καὶ τούτων αὖ ἕτερά ἐστιν εἴδη, καθʼ ἕκαστον αὐτῶν πειρασόμεθα διδάσκειν τὴν κλίσιν ἐπὶ παραδείγματος. ἡ μὲν οὖν ὀρθὴ οὐδεμίαν ἔχει δυσκολίαν κατὰ γὰρ αὐτὴν ἑκάστη τῶν χρειῶν εἴωθε προφέρεσθαι. τὴν δὲ γενικὴν πτῶσιν οὕτω κλινοῦμεν· ἐὰν μὲν λογικὴ χρεία, προσθήσομεν αὐτῇ, τὸ ῥηθὲν μνήμης ἔτυχεν, ἢ λόγος ἀπομνημονεύεται εἰπόντος. τὸ μὲν οὖν πρότερον μετὰ τὴν ἀπαγγελίαν ὅλης τῆς χρείας εὐπρεπές ἐστιν ἐπενεγκεῖν, οἷον Ἰσοκράτους τοῦ ῥήτορος τοὺς εὐφυεῖς τῶν μαθητῶν θεῶν παῖδας λέγοντος εἶναι τὸ ῥηθὲν μνήμης ἔτυχε, τὸ δὲ δεύτερον μεσούσης αὐτῆς καὶ τῆς ἀποφάσεως ἀρχομένης, οἷον Πιττακοῦ τοῦ Μιτυληναίου ἐρωτηθέντος εἰ λανθάνει τις τοὺς θεοὺς φαῦλόν τι ποιῶν, λόγος ἀπομνημονεύεται εἰπόντος, οὐδὲ διανοούμενος. ἁρμόττει δὲ μᾶλλον τὸ μέν, λόγος ἀπομνημονεύεται, πάσαις ταῖς λογικαῖς χρείαις, πλὴν τῆς καθʼ ἑκούσιον ἀπό φασιν· ταύτῃ γὰρ τὸ ῥηθὲν μνήμης ἔτυχεν. ἐὰν δὲ πρακτικὴ χρεία, εἰ μὲν παθητικὴ εἴη, προσθετέον, τὸ συμβὰν μνήμης ἔτυχεν. εἰ δὲ ἐνεργητική, τὸ πραχθὲν μνήμης ἔτυχεν, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ μικτοῦ. ἐπὶ τέλει μέντοι τῶν χρειῶν καὶ τούτων ἕκαστον προσθετέον, οἷον Διδύμου τοῦ αὐλητοῦ ἁλόντος ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ὀνόματος κρεμασθέντος τὸ συμβὰν μνήμης ἔτυχε, καὶ Διογένους τοῦ Κυνικοῦ φιλοσόφου ἰδόντος ὀψοφάγον παῖδα καὶ τὸν παιδαγωγὸν τῇ βακτηρίᾳ παίσαντος τὸ πραχθὲν μνήμης ἔτυχε. τῇ δὲ δοτικῇ ἐπὶ πάσης χρείας πλὴν τῆς παθητικῆς προσθήσομεν τὸ ἔδοξεν ἢ τὸ ἐφάνη ἢ τὸ ἐπῆλθεν ἢ καὶ τὸ παρέστη ἤ τι τῶν τοιούτων, οἷον Διογένει τῷ Κυνικῷ φιλοσόφῳ ἰδόντι μειράκιον πλούσιον ἀπαίδευτον ἔδοξεν εἰπεῖν, οὗτός ἐστι ῥύπος περιηργυρωμένος. ἐπὶ μὲν τῆς παθητικῆς προσθήσομεν τὸ συνέβη, οἷον Διδύμῳ τῷ αὐλητῇ ἁλόντι ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ συνέβη ἐκ τοῦ ὀνόματος κρεμασθῆναι. ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς αἰτιατικῆς προσθήσομεν καθόλου ἐπὶ πάσης χρείας τὸ φασί, τὸ λέγεται, οἷον Διογένην τὸν Κυνικὸν φιλόσοφον ἰδόντα μειράκιον πλούσιον ἀπαίδευτόν φασιν εἰπεῖν, ἢ λέγεται, οὗτός ἐστι ῥύπος περιηργυρωμένος. ἡ δὲ κλητικὴ σαφής ἐστι· ποιησόμεθα γὰρ τὸν λόγον πρὸς παρὸν ἡμῖν πρόσωπον, ἐφʼ ὃ ἡ χρεία ἀναφέρεται, οἷον Διόγενες Κυνικὲ φιλόσοφε, ἰδών μειράκιον πλούσιον ἀπαίδευτον, εἶπας, οὗτός ἐστι ῥύπος περιηργυρωμένος. ἐπιφωνεῖν δέ ἐστιν ἀποδεχομένους οἰκείως καὶ συντόμως τὸ εἰρημένον διὰ τῆς χρείας, ἢ ὡς ἀληθές ἐστιν, ἢ ὡς καλόν, ἢ ὡς συμφέρον, ἢ ὡς καὶ ἄλλοις τὸ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἔδοξεν ἀνδράσι δεδοκιμασμένοις, οἶον Εὐριπίδης ὁ ποιητὴς τὸν νοῦν ἡμῶν ἑκάστου ἔφησεν εἶναι θεόν. ἐπιφωνήσομεν δὲ ἐκ μὲν τοῦ ἀληθοῦς οὕτως· θεὸς γὰρ ὄντως ἑκάστῳ ὁ νοῦς, ἐφʼ ἃ μὲν συμφέρει προτρέπων ἡμὰς, ἀπείργων δὲ τῶν ζημιούντων. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ καλοῦ οὕτω· καλὸν γὰρ ἕκαστον μὴ ἐν χρυσῷ καὶ ἀργύρῳ νομίζειν εἶναι τὸν θεόν, ἀλλʼ ἐν ἑαυτῷ. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ συμφέροντος οὕτως· ἵνα μὴ διὰ μακροῦ κεῖσθαι τὸ τιμωροῦν οἰόμενοι πολλὴν τοῦ ἀδικεῖν ἔχοιμεν εὐχέρειαν. ἐκ δὲ τῆς τῶν εὐδοκίμων μαρτυρίας, ὅταν ἢ σοφὸν ἢ νομοθέτην ἢ ποιητὴν ἢ ἄλλον τινὰ τῶν διωνομασμένων λέγωμεν ὁμογνωμονεῖν τῷ ῥηθέντι, οἷον ἐπὶ τῆς προκειμένης χρείας φήσομεν· τοῖος γὰρ νόος ἐστὶν ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων, οἶον ἐπʼ ἦμαρ ἄγῃσι πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε. ἀντιλέγομεν δὲ ταῖς χρείαις ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων, ὡς πρὸς τὸν Ἰσοκράτην, εἰπόντα ὅτι τοὺς διδασκάλους προτιμητέον τῶν πατέρων· οἱ μὲν γὰρ τὸ ζῆν ἡμῖν, οἱ δὲ διδάσκαλοι τὸ καλῶς ζῆν παρέσχοντο. φαμὲν γὰρ ἀντιλέγοντες, ὅτι οὐκ ἐνῆν καλῶς ζῆν, εἰ μὴ τὸ ζῆν οἱ πατέρες παρέσχοντο. εἰδέναι δὲ δεῖ, ὅτι οὐ δυνατὸν ἀντιλέγειν πάσῃ χρείᾳ πολλῶν καλῶς καὶ ἀμέμπτως εἰρημένων, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ πάσας ἐστὶν ἐπαινεῖν διὰ τό τινων εὐθὺς προσπίπτειν τὴν ἀτοπίαν. ἐπεκτείνομεν δὲ τὴν χρείαν, ἐπειδὰν τὰς ἐν αὐτῇ ἐρωτήσεις τε καὶ ἀποκρίσεις, καὶ εἰ πρᾶξίς τις ἢ πάθος ἐνυπάρχῃ, μηκύνοιμεν. συστέλλομεν δὲ τὸ ἐναντίον ποιοῦντες, οἷον σύντομος μὲν χρεία Ἐπαμεινώνδας, ἄτεκνος ἀποθνήσκων, ἔλεγε τοῖς φίλοις, καὶ ἄλλων εἰς αὐτὴν δεόμεθα. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἀδυνάτου, ὡς ἄν φῶμεν πρὸς τὸν Ἰσοκράτην, μὴ δυνατὸν ἐκ θεῶν ἀνθρώπους γενέσθαι, μηδ’ ἂν εὐφυεῖς ὦσιν. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἀπιθάνου, ὅτι μὴ εἰκός ἐστιν, Ἀντισθένην Ἀττικόν γε ὄντα παραγενόμενον Ἀθήνηθεν εἰς Λακεδαίμονα ἐκ τῆς γυναικωνίτιδος λέγειν εἰς τὴν ἀνδρωνῖτιν ἐπιέναι. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ψευδοῦς, ὅτι μὴ ἀληθῶς ὁ Βίων ἔλεγε τὴν φιλαργυρίαν μητρόπολιν εἶναι τῆς κακίας· μᾶλλον γὰρ ἀφροσύνη ἐστίν. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἀσυμφόρου, ὅτι βλαβερῶς παραινεῖ Σιμωνίδης παίζειν ἐν τῷ βίῳ καὶ περὶ μηδὲν ἁπλῶς σπουδάζειν. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἀχρήστου, οἷον εἰ φαίνοιτο πρὸς οὐδὲν ὠφέλιμον τὸ ῥηθὲν τῷ βίῳ. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ αἰσχροῦ, ὁπόταν αἰσχρὰν καὶ ἐπονείδιστον ἀποφαίνωμεν τὴν χρείαν, οἷον ἀνὴρ Συβαρίτης ἰδὼν Λακεδαιμονίους ἐπιπόνως ζῶντας οὐ θαυμάζειν ἔφησεν, ὅτι ἐν τοῖς πολέμοις οὐκ ὀκνοῦσιν ἀποθνήσκειν, ἄμεινον γὰρ εἶναι τὸν θάνατον τοῦ τοιούτου βίου πάνυ γὰρ μαλακῶς καὶ οὐκ ἀνδρείου τρόπου τὴν ἀπόφασιν ἐποιήσατο. ἐκ μὲν οὖν τούτων ἀνασκευαστέον, πρὸς ἕκαστον δὲ μέρος τῆς χρείας ἀρξάμενον ἀπὸ τῶν πρώτων ἐπιχειρεῖν δεῖ, ἐξ ὅσων τόπων ἄν δυνατὸν ᾖ μὴ λανθανέτω γὰρ ἡμᾶς ὅτι οὐχ οἷόν τέ ἐστιν ἐν πάσαις ἐκ πάντων ἐπιχειρεῖν.
verses.heading: The exercises: recitation, inflection, comment, objection

verses.text: We shall arrange the arguments in the same order in which we set out the topics; and the same topics would serve also for the refutation and the confirmation of maxims. Those who are already more advanced should take their starting points from what we shall set out for the theses as well. The introduction must not be of such a kind as to fit other chreiai, but proper to the one at hand; and this will be done well, in the case of the chreia and the fable and all the rest, when we take the starting points of our introductions from one or two of the highest divisions. After the introduction one must set out the chreia itself, and then the arguments in order. Here one should use amplifications and digressions and characterizations, wherever they are possible.
verses.greek: Τὴν μέντοι τάξιν τῶν ἐπιχειρημάτων ποιησόμεθα, καθὰ καὶ τῶν τόπων ἐκτιθέμεθα, οἱ αὐτοὶ δʼ ἂν εἶεν καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν γνωμῶν ἀνασκευήν τε καὶ κατασκευήν. τοῖς δὲ ἤδη τελειοτέροις προσήκει τὰς ἀφορμὰς λαμβάνειν καὶ ἐκ τῶν πρὸς τὰς θέσεις ἡμῖν παραθησομένων. χρὴ δὲ τὸ προοίμιον μὴ τοιοῦτον εἶναι, ὥστε ἐφαρμόττειν ἑτέραις χρείαις, ἀλλʼ ἴδιον τῆς ὑποκειμένης. τοῦτο δʼ ἂν καλῶς γένοιτο ἐπί τε χρείας καὶ μύθου καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων, ὅταν ἐξ ἑνὸς ἢ δύο τῶν ἀνωτάτω μερῶν τὰς ἀφορμὰς τῶν προοιμίων λαμβάνωμεν. μετὰ δὲ τὸ προοίμιον αὐτήν τε τὴν χρείαν ἐκθετέον, εἶτα ἑξῆς τὰς ἐπιχειρήσεις. χρηστέον δὲ ἐνταῦθα καὶ αὐξήσεσι καὶ παρεκβάσεσι καὶ ἤθεσιν, οἷς δυνατόν ἐστιν.
